Who led the rebuilding of Lisbon?
Which Enlightenment writer questioned divine goodness after the disaster?
quiz.explain: In his poem and in Candide.

lessons.title: The age of revolutions
lessons.summary: America, France, Napoleon and Portugal.

cards.title: The American Revolution
cards.text: Thirteen British colonies rebelled over taxation without representation. The Declaration of Independence (1776) proclaimed that all men are created equal, though slavery continued.

deep.x: After the Seven Years' War (1756–63), Britain was deep in debt and decided the American colonies should help pay for their own defence. Colonists objected not so much to the size of the taxes as to the principle: they had no members in the British Parliament that voted them.
From protest to war

Fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. On 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. It argued, in the language of Locke, that people have rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and may replace a government that destroys them.
Why the colonists won

x: France joined in 1778 after the American victory at Saratoga, followed by Spain
The British had to fight across a huge territory, 5,000 km from home
The French fleet helped trap the British army at Yorktown in 1781

deep.x: The contradiction

About one in five people in the colonies was enslaved. Jefferson himself enslaved hundreds of people over his lifetime. The equality the Declaration promised did not reach enslaved Africans, Native Americans or women; Black Americans would wait until the 1860s for abolition and the 1960s for full civil rights.
The American Revolution put the idea that government rests on the consent of the governed into practice for the first time on a large scale.
France's spending on the American war worsened its own debt crisis, helping to trigger the French Revolution a few years later.

cards.title: The French Revolution
cards.text: In 1789, with France bankrupt and bread expensive, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and Parisians stormed the Bastille. Feudal privileges were abolished.

deep.x: France in 1789 was rich but its government was broke. Wars, including support for the Americans, had piled up debt, and interest payments swallowed a huge share of the budget. The nobles and clergy largely escaped taxation, so the king needed their consent for reform, and they refused.
Bread and anger

Bad harvests in 1788 pushed bread prices to record levels. A labourer could spend more than half his daily wage on bread alone. Hunger in the cities and resentment of feudal dues in the countryside made people ready to act.
How it unfolded

Louis XVI called the Estates-General for the first time since 1614. When the Third Estate was outvoted, its deputies declared themselves the National Assembly and swore not to separate until France had a constitution. On 14 July, Parisians stormed the Bastille, a fortress-prison and symbol of royal power, to seize gunpowder.

x: On the night of 4 August, the Assembly abolished feudal privileges
Church lands were nationalised to pay the debt
The monarchy was abolished in 1792, and Louis XVI executed in January 1793

deep.x: The French Revolution replaced a society of inherited ranks with the idea of equal citizens.

deep.w: The Bastille was full of political prisoners
deep.r: It held only seven prisoners on 14 July 1789; its capture mattered as a symbol

cards.title: Liberty, equality, fraternity
cards.text: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) proclaimed equality before the law, freedom of speech and the sovereignty of the nation, ideas that spread worldwide.

deep.x: Adopted on 26 August 1789, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen has 17 short articles. Its first states that men are born and remain free and equal in rights. It drew on Enlightenment thinkers and on the American example; Lafayette, who had fought in America, helped draft it.

items: Taxes shared by ability to pay

deep.x: Who was left out?

The "rights of man" did not, in practice, include women. In 1791 the playwright Olympe de Gouges answered with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman; she was guillotined in 1793. France abolished slavery in its colonies in 1794, after a slave uprising in Saint-Domingue, but Napoleon restored it in 1802. Saint-Domingue fought on and became independent Haiti in 1804.
How the ideas travelled
Portugal's first constitution, in 1822, borrowed directly from this language. The 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights carry the same core ideas.
The Declaration of 1789 turned privileges for some into rights for all, at least on paper, and set a standard people could demand.
The motto "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" was used during the Revolution but became France's official motto only in the late 19th century.

cards.title: The Terror
cards.text: In 1793–94, the revolutionary government executed thousands of suspected enemies by guillotine, including many revolutionaries themselves, until Robespierre himself was executed.

deep.x: By 1793 France was at war with much of Europe, facing a royalist uprising in the Vendée in the west, and short of food. The radical Jacobins argued that the Revolution could survive only by crushing its enemies at home. A Committee of Public Safety, increasingly led by Maximilien Robespierre, took emergency powers.
How it worked

The Law of Suspects (September 1793) allowed the arrest of almost anyone suspected of disloyalty. Trials became quick and the defence limited. Victims included Queen Marie Antoinette, the moderate Girondins, Olympe de Gouges, the chemist Lavoisier and finally revolutionaries like Danton.
Many more died in prison or were killed without trial, and the repression of the Vendée cost tens of thousands of lives, perhaps far more; the totals are disputed.
The end
On 27 July 1794 (9 Thermidor in the revolutionary calendar), fellow deputies afraid they would be next turned on Robespierre. He was guillotined the following day.

x: The word "terrorism" comes from this period
The guillotine was meant to be humane and equal: one quick death for all classes

deep.x: The Terror showed how a revolution for rights can turn on its own people when fear rules.

deep.w: Most victims were nobles
deep.r: Most were ordinary people: peasants, workers and townspeople, not aristocrats

cards.title: Napoleon
cards.text: Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804 and conquered much of Europe. His Napoleonic Code influenced law across Europe, including Portugal.

deep.x: Born in Corsica in 1769, Napoleon Bonaparte rose fast in the revolutionary army, which promoted talent rather than birth. Victories in Italy made him a hero. In November 1799 he took power in a coup, and in 1804 he crowned himself emperor in Notre-Dame, taking the crown from the Pope's hands.
The Napoleonic Code

The Civil Code of 1804 replaced hundreds of local laws with one clear, written system. It guaranteed equality before the law, secure property and civil marriage, and ended feudal rights. But it also made wives legally subordinate to their husbands.
Portugal's first Civil Code of 1867 drew on it, as did codes in Spain, Italy, Belgium and Latin America. The metric system also spread with French armies.
Rise and fall

x: At its peak around 1810–12, Napoleon controlled or dominated most of continental Europe
About 600,000 soldiers invaded Russia in 1812; only a fraction came back
Defeated at Leipzig (1813) and exiled to Elba, he returned for 100 days before Waterloo

deep.x: He died in exile on Saint Helena in 1821.
Napoleon spread the Revolution's legal ideas across Europe while destroying its democracy at home.

deep.w: Napoleon was unusually short
deep.r: He was about 1.69 m, average for his time; British cartoons and old French measures created the myth

cards.title: The French invasions of Portugal
cards.text: Because Portugal kept trading with Britain, Napoleon invaded three times from 1807. With British help under Wellington, the Portuguese resisted, including at the Lines of Torres Vedras.

deep.x: In 1806 Napoleon ordered a Continental Blockade: no European country should trade with Britain. Portugal, Britain's oldest ally and dependent on British trade, could not comply. In late 1807 a French army under General Junot marched through Spain towards Lisbon.
Three invasions

x: 1807–08: Junot occupied Lisbon; British troops landed and won at Vimeiro
1809: Soult invaded the north; as Porto fell, a pontoon bridge over the Douro collapsed under fleeing crowds and many drowned
1810–11: Masséna was checked at Buçaco, then stopped by the Lines of Torres Vedras

deep.x: The Lines of Torres Vedras

Wellington had thousands of Portuguese labourers secretly build three lines of forts, redoubts and blocked valleys across the peninsula north of Lisbon. When Masséna arrived in October 1810, he found them impossible to break.

The countryside in front of the lines had been stripped of food and people. The French waited for months, hungry, and then retreated, losing many men. The scorched-earth tactic saved Lisbon but caused great suffering for Portuguese civilians.
Portugal survived Napoleon through British alliance, a fortified line and the endurance of its people, at a heavy civilian cost.
The phrase "ficar a ver navios" (to be left watching ships) is popularly linked to Junot arriving in Lisbon just as the royal fleet sailed away.

cards.title: The court flees to Brazil
cards.text: In 1807, as the French approached, the royal family and thousands of courtiers sailed to Brazil. Rio de Janeiro became the capital of the Portuguese empire, the only time a European capital moved to a colony.

deep.x: With Junot's army days from Lisbon, Prince Regent João, who ruled for his mentally ill mother Queen Maria I, made a radical choice: rather than be captured, he moved the whole government across the Atlantic. The fleet left on 29 November 1807, escorted by the British navy; the French entered Lisbon the next day.
Rio transformed
The court arrived in Salvador in January 1808 and settled in Rio de Janeiro in March. A colonial town suddenly hosted ministries, courts and a royal household.
A colony becomes a kingdom

In 1815 Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal with Portugal: the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves. For Brazilians this was a huge step up. For many in Portugal it felt like the opposite: the mother country governed from its colony, with a British marshal, Beresford, running the army at home.
By moving the court to Rio, Portugal saved its monarchy but set Brazil on the road to independence.
Rio was the only European capital ever transferred to a colony, and Maria I became the first reigning European monarch to set foot in the Americas.

cards.title: Brazil's independence
cards.text: After the king returned to Portugal, his son Pedro stayed in Brazil and declared independence on 7 September 1822, becoming Emperor Pedro I.

deep.x: The Liberal Revolution of 1820 in Portugal demanded the king's return, and João VI sailed back to Lisbon in 1821. He left his son Pedro as regent in Rio. The new Portuguese parliament then tried to reduce Brazil to colonial status again, which angered Brazil's elites.
"Independence or death"

When Lisbon ordered Pedro home, he refused in January 1822 (the "Dia do Fico", "I'm staying" day). On 7 September 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga stream near São Paulo, he received new orders from Lisbon and declared independence. He was crowned Emperor Pedro I in December.
Different from Spanish America
Because a member of the royal family led independence, Brazil kept its unity and a monarchy until 1889. Slavery also continued, which suited the landowning elite.
One man, two crowns

In 1826 Pedro inherited the Portuguese throne as Pedro IV. He gave Portugal a constitutional charter, then abdicated in favour of his young daughter, Maria II, which sparked conflict with his brother Miguel.
Brazil's independence was led by the heir to Portugal's own throne, which made it unusually peaceful and kept the country united.
Portugal recognised Brazil's independence in 1825 only after Brazil agreed to pay compensation, largely by taking on a Portuguese debt owed to Britain.

cards.title: The Liberal Revolution
cards.text: The 1820 revolution in Porto demanded a constitution. A civil war (1828–1834) between liberals under Pedro and absolutists under his brother Miguel ended with the liberals' victory.

deep.x: In 1820 Portugal was in a strange state: the king lived in Brazil, the army was run by a British marshal, and trade had collapsed. On 24 August 1820, military officers and merchants in Porto rose up and called for a parliament (Cortes) and a written constitution.
Two brothers, two visions
Miguel, backed by the Church, most nobles and much of the countryside, was acclaimed absolute king in 1828. Pedro gave up the Brazilian crown in 1831 and came to fight for his daughter's rights.
The siege of Porto

Pedro landed near Porto in July 1832 with about 7,500 men. Miguel's much larger army besieged the city for about a year. Porto held out through hunger, cholera and bombardment, which is why it is still called "a Cidade Invicta", the unconquered city. Liberal victories at sea and on land ended the war with the agreement of Évora Monte in 1834.

x: Miguel went into exile
Religious orders were dissolved and their property sold
Pedro died in 1834, only months after victory

deep.x: The civil war decided that Portugal would be a constitutional monarchy, not an absolute one.
Pedro left his heart to Porto in gratitude. It is kept in the Lapa church in the city.

cards.title: Revolutions in Latin America
cards.text: Inspired by the US and France, and helped by Spain's weakness under Napoleon, most of Spanish America won independence between 1810 and 1825, led by figures like Simón Bolívar.

deep.x: In 1808 Napoleon forced the Spanish king to abdicate and put his brother Joseph on the throne. In the colonies, local elites asked who now had authority. Many formed their own governing councils in 1810, at first claiming loyalty to the captive king. They soon moved towards independence.
The creole elite

Leadership came mostly from creoles, people of Spanish descent born in America, who resented that the top posts went to Spaniards. They read Enlightenment books and knew the American and French examples. Enslaved people, Indigenous peoples and mixed-race soldiers did much of the fighting, often with promises that were only partly kept.
Leaders
San Martín led an army across the Andes in 1817, one of the boldest marches in military history. The battle of Ayacucho in Peru (1824) effectively ended Spanish rule on the mainland.
What came after

x: Bolívar dreamed of a united Spanish America, but Gran Colombia split in 1830
Many new republics suffered decades of civil wars and strongmen
Cuba and Puerto Rico stayed Spanish until 1898

deep.x: Napoleon's invasion of Spain opened the door, but Latin Americans themselves fought for and won their independence.
Bolivia is named after Simón Bolívar, who was its first president.

quiz.q: Why did Napoleon invade Portugal?
options: Portugal kept trading with Britain against his blockade

quiz.q: Where did the Portuguese court move in 1807?
When did Brazil declare independence?

lessons.title: The 19th century
lessons.summary: Industry, railways, empires and new ideas.

cards.title: Railways
cards.text: The first public steam railway opened in England in 1825. Railways shrank journeys from days to hours and opened markets. Portugal's first line, Lisbon to Carregado, opened in 1856.

deep.x: The railway combined two older ideas: wagons on rails, used in mines for centuries, and the steam engine. In 1825 George Stephenson's locomotive pulled the first public steam train on the Stockton and Darlington line in north-east England. In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway became the first intercity line run entirely by steam.
What railways changed

x: Fresh food, coal and post moved fast and cheaply, so prices fell
Towns along the line grew; towns bypassed often declined
Ordinary people could travel for work or leisure, inventing the day trip and the seaside holiday
Clocks were standardised: Britain adopted "railway time" in the 1840s so timetables made sense

deep.x: Portugal gets on board

Portugal came later. Under the "Regeneração" governments, minister Fontes Pereira de Melo pushed roads and railways to modernise the country. The first line, about 36 km from Lisbon to Carregado, opened on 28 October 1856. By 1864 trains linked Lisbon with Porto (at Gaia), and in 1877 Gustave Eiffel's company finished the Maria Pia bridge across the Douro so trains could enter Porto.
Railways shrank distances, created national markets and made time itself uniform.
Portugal and Spain use a wider track gauge (about 1.67 m) than most of Europe (1.435 m), one reason Iberian trains long had to stop or change axles at the French border.

cards.title: Steamships and telegraph

viz.unit: days for a London–New York message

cards.text: Steamships made ocean travel reliable, and the telegraph carried messages instantly. The first lasting transatlantic cable (1866) cut message times from weeks to minutes.

deep.x: Sailing ships depended on the wind and could be stuck for days in calm seas. Steamships kept schedules. From the 1840s regular steam lines crossed the Atlantic in about two weeks, and iron hulls and the screw propeller made ships bigger and faster through the century.
Coal and islands

Steamers needed coal every few thousand kilometres. Atlantic islands became filling stations: Madeira, and above all Mindelo on São Vicente in Cape Verde, grew busy supplying British ships on their way to South America and Africa.
The Victorian internet

The electric telegraph sent coded pulses along a wire. Samuel Morse's code and his first long line in the USA (1844) showed it worked. Undersea cables followed. A transatlantic cable of 1858 failed within weeks; in 1866 the giant ship Great Eastern laid one that lasted.

v.unit: London to New York message time

deep.x: Portugal as a cable hub

In 1870 a cable station at Carcavelos, near Lisbon, linked Britain with Gibraltar, Malta and India. Later, Horta on the island of Faial in the Azores became a crossroads of transatlantic cables, with operators from several countries living there.
Steam and the telegraph separated information from transport: news could now travel far faster than people or goods.
Governments and newspapers could now learn of wars and market prices in minutes, and stock exchanges in London and New York began to move together.

cards.title: Cities and factories
cards.text: Millions moved from farms to industrial cities. Conditions were harsh: long hours, child labour, crowded housing and polluted air. Reforms, unions and new laws slowly improved them.

deep.x: Factories needed workers in one place, near coal, water and transport. Farm workers, pushed by poverty and pulled by wages, moved in. By 1851 Britain became the first country where more people lived in towns than in the countryside. Manchester grew from a market town into the world's first great industrial city.
Life in the industrial city

x: Working days of 12–14 hours, six days a week, were normal
Children worked in mills and mines, crawling under machines and pulling coal carts
Whole families lived in single rooms, sharing outdoor toilets
Cholera spread through dirty water; in 1854 John Snow traced a London outbreak to one water pump

deep.x: How things improved

Reforms came from campaigners, doctors, journalists and novelists like Charles Dickens, and from workers organising unions and strikes. Sewers, clean water and building rules eventually made cities healthier.
Portugal's slower path

Portugal industrialised late and on a smaller scale. Textile mills grew in Porto, the Ave valley and Covilhã, where wool was spun from mountain sheep, and Lisbon had tobacco, cork and metal works. Portugal set an eight-hour working day for industry in 1919.
Industry made more goods than ever before, but it took decades of struggle to make industrial cities fit to live in.

deep.w: Child labour began in factories
deep.r: Children had always worked on farms; factories made it more visible and more dangerous, which drove the first laws

cards.title: New ideologies
cards.text: The 19th century produced liberalism, nationalism, socialism and Marxism, ideas about the state, nations and workers that shaped the next century.

deep.x: Industry, cities and the French Revolution raised new questions. Who should rule? What holds a nation together? Why are workers poor in such a rich society? The 19th century answered with "-isms" that still shape politics today.
1848: the springtime of peoples

In 1848 revolutions broke out in Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest and elsewhere. Liberals wanted constitutions, nationalists wanted their own states, and workers wanted jobs and votes. Most uprisings were crushed within a year, but France gained universal male suffrage and serfdom ended in the Austrian Empire.
Marx and Marxism

In the same year Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the Communist Manifesto. Marx argued that history is a struggle between classes, and that capitalism would be overthrown by the workers it exploited.
Others disagreed on the route: social democrats wanted reforms through elections and unions; anarchists wanted to abolish the state altogether.
In Portugal

x: The Portuguese Socialist Party was founded in 1875
The Republican Party (1876) mixed liberal, nationalist and anticlerical ideas
Republicanism won in 1910, when the monarchy fell

deep.x: The big political families of today, from liberal to socialist and nationalist, were born in the 19th century.
The terms "left" and "right" come from the French Revolution, when supporters of change sat on the left of the assembly's president.

cards.title: Abolition of slavery
cards.text: Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1833. Portugal abolished slavery in stages, completing it in 1869–1878; Brazil was the last in the Americas, in 1888.

deep.x: Between the 1500s and the 1860s, about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships crossing the Atlantic, and about 10.7 million survived the voyage. Ships under the Portuguese and Brazilian flags carried the largest share, close to half of them, mostly to Brazil.
Why abolition happened

Enlightenment and religious arguments, especially from Quakers and evangelicals like William Wilberforce, slowly turned opinion. Enslaved people resisted constantly; the Haitian revolution and major revolts in Jamaica raised the cost of slavery. Economic changes mattered too, though historians debate how much.
Portugal's slow steps

After 1869, people were renamed "libertos" but still had to work for their former owners until 1878. Even after that, forced labour schemes in the African colonies continued well into the 20th century, until the early 1960s.
Compensation for whom?

When Britain ended slavery in 1833, it paid £20 million to slave owners, about 40% of the government's yearly budget. Enslaved people received nothing and were made to work as unpaid "apprentices" for several more years.
Abolition took over 80 years across the Atlantic world, and it often compensated owners rather than the enslaved.

deep.w: Slavery ended the day it was abolished
deep.r: Forced labour, debt bondage and legal discrimination often continued for generations

cards.title: The Scramble for Africa
cards.text: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European powers set rules for dividing Africa. By 1914, almost the whole continent was under European control.

deep.x: In 1870 Europeans controlled only about a tenth of Africa, mostly along the coasts. Portugal held old trading footholds in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea. Within 40 years almost the whole continent was divided up.
The Berlin Conference

Germany's chancellor Bismarck hosted European powers and the USA in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885. No Africans were invited. The conference set the rule of "effective occupation": to claim territory, a power had to actually control it, which triggered a rush to send soldiers, officials and treaties inland.
Why it was possible now
The consequences

x: Borders often ignored existing peoples and kingdoms; many were drawn as straight lines on maps
Colonies were run to extract rubber, minerals, cotton and labour
In King Leopold II's Congo Free State, forced labour for rubber caused mass deaths, probably in the millions
Only Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia remained independent

deep.x: The Scramble for Africa was decided around European tables, and its borders still frame African states today.
Most of today's African borders were set in this period; after independence, African states agreed in 1964 to keep them to avoid endless wars.

cards.title: The Pink Map and the Ultimatum
cards.text: Portugal hoped to link Angola and Mozambique (the "Pink Map"). Britain, wanting a Cape-to-Cairo route, issued the 1890 Ultimatum, forcing Portugal to back down, a national humiliation that fuelled republicanism.

deep.x: Portugal had coastal colonies on both sides of southern Africa: Angola on the Atlantic and Mozambique on the Indian Ocean. Explorers such as Serpa Pinto, and Capelo and Ivens, crossed the continent in the 1870s and 1880s. In 1886 Portugal published a map showing a belt of pink linking the two: the "Mapa Cor-de-Rosa".
The collision

The two plans crossed in the lands that are now Zambia, Zimbabwe and Malawi. British businessman Cecil Rhodes wanted that territory, and the British government backed him. On 11 January 1890 Britain sent Portugal an ultimatum: withdraw its forces or face the Royal Navy. Portugal, with no hope of winning, gave in.
A national humiliation

Britain was Portugal's oldest ally, so the shock was enormous. Crowds protested, British goods were boycotted and writers like Guerra Junqueiro attacked King Carlos. Many blamed the monarchy for weakness. In 1891 republicans in Porto attempted a revolt, which failed.
The 1890 Ultimatum turned colonial frustration into anger at the monarchy and helped bring the republic two decades later.
Portugal's national anthem, "A Portuguesa", was written in 1890 in response to the Ultimatum; an early version called on people to march against the British, later changed to "against the cannons".

cards.title: Science and medicine
cards.text: Darwin's theory of evolution (1859), Pasteur's germ theory, vaccines, anaesthesia and antiseptic surgery transformed biology and medicine.

deep.x: In 1800, surgery was done without anaesthesia, nobody knew that germs cause disease, and most people believed species had been created unchanged. By 1900 all three ideas had been overturned.
Evolution

In On the Origin of Species (1859), Charles Darwin argued that living things change over generations by natural selection. Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently. Gregor Mendel's pea experiments (1866) showed how traits are inherited, though they were ignored until 1900.
Germs and medicine

Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and decay, and that heating kills them, the origin of pasteurised milk. Robert Koch identified the bacteria behind anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera. Joseph Lister used carbolic acid to clean wounds and instruments, and deaths after surgery fell sharply.
In the 1840s Ignaz Semmelweis made doctors in his Vienna clinic wash their hands, and deaths of new mothers fell from around 10% to under 2%. Colleagues mocked him.
Portugal's part
In 1899 the doctor Ricardo Jorge identified bubonic plague in Porto and imposed a quarantine. It was unpopular, but it helped contain the outbreak and led to Portugal's modern public health service.
The 19th century discovered how life changes and how disease spreads, laying the foundations of modern biology and medicine.

deep.w: Darwin said humans descend from monkeys
deep.r: Humans and other apes share a common ancestor; neither descends from the other

cards.title: Unification of Italy and Germany
cards.text: Italy unified between 1859 and 1871 and Germany in 1871 under Prussia, changing Europe's balance of power and setting the stage for rivalries before 1914.

deep.x: In 1850, "Italy" and "Germany" were ideas rather than states. Italy was split into kingdoms, duchies and the Papal States, with Austria ruling the north-east. Germans lived in nearly 40 states loosely tied together, the biggest being Prussia and Austria.
Italy

Piedmont's prime minister Cavour won French help against Austria in 1859. In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi and his "Thousand" volunteers conquered Sicily and Naples, then handed them to the king of Piedmont. The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, took Venice in 1866 and Rome in 1870, which became its capital in 1871.
Germany
Prussia's chancellor Otto von Bismarck said Germany would be united not by speeches but by "blood and iron". Three short wars did it:
The German Empire was proclaimed in January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, a deliberate humiliation of France, which also lost Alsace and Lorraine.
A new balance

x: Germany quickly became Europe's leading industrial and military power
France wanted revenge and its lost provinces back
Bismarck built alliances to isolate France; after he left in 1890, rivalries hardened into two blocs

deep.x: Two new great powers in the heart of Europe upset the old balance and planted rivalries that exploded in 1914.
When Italy unified, only a small minority of its people spoke standard Italian at home; most used regional languages and dialects.

cards.title: Electricity and the telephone
cards.text: In the last decades of the century came the telephone (1876), the light bulb (1879), electric power stations, cars (1886) and radio, the foundations of the 20th century.

deep.x: Electricity was studied for centuries, but only after Michael Faraday showed in 1831 how moving magnets create electric current could it be produced on a large scale. In the last quarter of the 19th century, a cluster of inventions turned it into everyday technology.
Who invented what?

Inventions often had several parents. Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876, but others, including Antonio Meucci and Elisha Gray, worked on similar devices. Thomas Edison in the USA and Joseph Swan in Britain both made working light bulbs around 1879. Edison's genius was the whole system: power station, cables, meters and bulbs.
The war of the currents
AC won, because transformers let it travel far at high voltage and then be stepped down safely. Our sockets still use it: 230 volts at 50 hertz in Portugal.
Portugal lights up
In 1878 electric lamps lit the citadel of Cascais for the birthday of the future King Carlos, the first electric lighting in Portugal. Lisbon's first electric trams ran in 1901.
Electricity turned energy into something that could be sent down a wire to every home and factory, the base of 20th-century life.
Before electric light, the working day for most people ended with sunset; cheap lighting changed how long people worked, studied and socialised.

quiz.q: When did Portugal's first railway open?
What was the 1890 British Ultimatum about?
options: Portugal's plan to link Angola and Mozambique

quiz.q: Which country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery?

lessons.title: World War I
lessons.summary: The Great War, 1914–1918.

cards.title: The spark
cards.text: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was assassinated in Sarajevo. Alliances, militarism and rivalry turned a regional crisis into a world war within weeks.

deep.x: On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, visited Sarajevo, capital of Bosnia, which Austria had annexed in 1908. A group of young Bosnian Serb nationalists, armed with help from a secret Serbian network, lay in wait. A bomb missed. Later the archduke's driver took a wrong turn, and 19-year-old Gavrilo Princip shot the archduke and his wife Sophie.
From murder to world war

Austria-Hungary, with Germany's promise of support, sent Serbia an ultimatum designed to be rejected. Russia backed Serbia. Germany's war plan, the Schlieffen Plan, required knocking out France quickly through Belgium before Russia could mobilise. Invading neutral Belgium brought Britain in.
The deeper causes
Historians often summarise them as four forces:
The assassination was the spark; alliances, war plans and rivalry were the fuel.

deep.w: The war was inevitable after Sarajevo
deep.r: Leaders made choices for five weeks; historians still debate how much blame lies with Germany and Austria-Hungary

cards.title: Two alliances
cards.text: The Allies (France, Britain, Russia, later Italy, the USA and others including Portugal) fought the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Bulgaria).

deep.x: Before 1914, Europe's great powers had settled into two blocs. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy formed the Triple Alliance in 1882. France and Russia allied in 1894, and Britain, worried by Germany's growing navy, reached understandings with France (1904) and Russia (1907): the Triple Entente.
Changing sides and joining late

x: Italy stayed out in 1914, then joined the Allies in 1915, promised Austrian lands
The Ottoman Empire joined Germany in late 1914, opening fronts in the Middle East and at Gallipoli
Bulgaria joined the Central Powers in 1915; Romania and Greece joined the Allies
Japan joined the Allies and took Germany's colonies in China and the Pacific

deep.x: How Portugal entered

Portugal was already fighting German forces in Africa from 1914, but was not formally at war in Europe. In February 1916, at Britain's request, Portugal seized dozens of German merchant ships sheltering in its ports. Germany declared war on Portugal on 9 March 1916.
Alliances meant to deter war instead turned a Balkan crisis into a war of every great power.
By 1918 more than 25 countries were on the Allied side, from Brazil and China to Siam (Thailand).

cards.title: Trench warfare
cards.text: On the Western Front, armies dug trenches from the Channel to Switzerland. Machine guns and artillery made attacks deadly; battles like the Somme cost hundreds of thousands of lives for a few kilometres.

deep.x: In autumn 1914 both sides tried to outflank each other until the line reached the sea. Soldiers dug in to survive. The result was a line of trenches about 700 km long, from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border, that barely moved for three and a half years.
Why attacks failed

Defenders had machine guns firing hundreds of rounds a minute, barbed wire and dugouts deep enough to survive shelling. Attackers had to cross open "no man's land" on foot. Even when they broke into enemy trenches, reserves arrived by rail faster than the attackers could advance on foot.
The Somme

On 1 July 1916 the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties, nearly 20,000 of them killed, the worst day in its history. By November, more than a million men on both sides had been killed or wounded, and the Allies had advanced about 10 km.
Daily life
Most time in the trenches was boredom, mud, rats, lice and cold, broken by shelling and raids. Units rotated: a few days at the front, then support, then rest.
On the Western Front, defence was stronger than attack, so armies paid enormous prices for tiny gains.

deep.w: Soldiers spent years without leaving the front line
deep.r: Most rotated in and out every few days, though some units, like the Portuguese, were kept in the line for far too long

cards.title: New weapons
cards.text: WWI introduced poison gas, tanks, warplanes, submarines and industrial-scale artillery. War had become mechanised.

deep.x: The First World War was the first great war of the industrial age. Factories produced shells, guns and chemicals on a scale never seen, and both sides searched for weapons that could break the deadlock of the trenches.
Gas

Germany first used chlorine on a large scale at Ypres in April 1915; soon both sides used gas. Mustard gas burned skin and lungs. Gas masks quickly limited its effect: gas caused perhaps 90,000 deaths, a small share of the total, but it terrified soldiers and was later banned by the 1925 Geneva Protocol.
Tanks, planes and submarines

x: Early tanks were slow (about 6 km/h) and broke down often, but by 1918 they helped break German lines
Planes started as scouts; by 1918 there were fighter squadrons and bombing raids on cities
German U-boats sank thousands of merchant ships and nearly starved Britain in 1917

deep.x: The deadliest weapon
Artillery was the real killer: shells and shrapnel caused the majority of wounds. Millions of tonnes of shells were fired, and farmers in France and Belgium still dig up unexploded ones every year.
Industry made war mechanical: the side with more factories, not the bravest soldiers, had the advantage.
The British called the first tanks "water carriers" or "tanks" as a cover story to keep the weapon secret; the name stuck.

cards.title: Portugal at war
cards.text: Portugal fought in Africa to defend Angola and Mozambique, and from 1917 sent the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps to Flanders. At La Lys on 9 April 1918, Portuguese forces suffered heavy losses.

deep.x: The young Republic had several reasons to fight: to protect Angola and Mozambique, which Germany and Britain had discussed dividing; to keep Britain's support; and to win respect for a regime many European monarchies distrusted. Many Portuguese, including monarchists and much of the army, opposed going to war.
Africa

German forces from South West Africa (now Namibia) clashed with Portuguese troops in southern Angola from 1914. In northern Mozambique, Portuguese forces faced German East Africa's skilled commander Lettow-Vorbeck. Disease, heat and poor supplies killed more Portuguese soldiers than combat, and many African soldiers and porters died too.
Flanders

From early 1917 about 55,000 men of the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps (CEP) went to France. Poorly equipped and rarely relieved, morale sank, especially after Sidónio Pais took power in December 1917 and lost interest in the war.
La Lys, 9 April 1918
On the morning the exhausted Portuguese 2nd Division was due to be relieved, German forces attacked in overwhelming numbers. In a few hours, over 7,000 men were killed, wounded or captured.
Portugal entered the war for its empire and its Republic, and paid heavily in Africa and Flanders.
Private Aníbal Milhais held off German attackers with his machine gun at La Lys and became a hero; his commander reportedly said he was worth a million, hence his nickname "Soldado Milhões".

cards.title: The home front
cards.text: Whole economies served the war. Women took over factory and farm work, food was rationed and governments controlled production and news.

deep.x: This was "total war": victory depended on factories, farms and civilians as much as soldiers. Governments took powers they had never had in peacetime, controlling industry, food, transport and information.
Women at work

With millions of men at the front, women filled jobs in munitions factories, transport, offices and farms. In Britain, nearly a million women worked making munitions; many were poisoned by the chemicals, and their skin turned yellow. After the war many were pushed out of these jobs, but votes for women followed in Britain (1918, women over 30) and Germany (1918).
Hunger

Britain's naval blockade caused severe shortages in Germany and Austria-Hungary. In the winter of 1916–17, when potatoes failed, many Germans lived largely on turnips. Hunger and related illnesses killed hundreds of thousands of German civilians.
In Portugal
Food shortages and rising prices hit Portuguese cities hard. In 1917 hungry crowds in Lisbon attacked shops and warehouses, the so-called "potato revolt", and strikes spread.
In total war, the whole of society becomes part of the war machine, and its strains can topple governments.
To save fuel, Germany introduced daylight saving time in 1916; Britain, Portugal and others followed within weeks.

cards.title: The USA joins
cards.text: German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann telegram drew the USA into the war in 1917. Fresh American troops helped tip the balance in 1918. Russia left the war after its revolution.

deep.x: In 1914 the USA declared neutrality, and most Americans wanted to stay out. But American banks lent heavily to Britain and France, and American goods fed the Allies. Germany's U-boats, trying to cut that lifeline, kept killing Americans at sea.
The Zimmermann telegram

In January 1917 Germany's foreign minister sent a coded message to Mexico: if the USA entered the war, Mexico should attack it and recover Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. British code-breakers intercepted and decoded it, and its publication outraged Americans.
Russia exits

In March 1917 a revolution forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate. In November, the Bolsheviks under Lenin seized power, promising "peace, land and bread". In March 1918 they signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, giving up vast territories.
The race of 1918

Germany gambled on massive spring offensives in 1918 before the Americans arrived in strength. They gained ground but exhausted the army. From August the Allies counter-attacked; by autumn Germany's allies collapsed, and an armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918.
The USA's entry and Russia's exit reshaped the war, and 1918 became a race Germany lost.

deep.w: American troops won the war
deep.r: They tipped the balance in 1918, but France and Britain had done most of the fighting for four years

cards.title: The human cost
cards.text: Around 9–10 million soldiers and millions of civilians died. Then the 1918 flu pandemic killed tens of millions more worldwide.

deep.x: No war before had killed so many soldiers. Around 65 million men were mobilised; about 9–10 million died and around 20 million were wounded, many disabled for life. Civilians died from massacres, hunger and disease.
A lost generation

France lost about one in six of the men it mobilised. Villages across Europe lost most of their young men; war memorials in almost every town list them. Survivors came back with missing limbs, disfigured faces and "shell shock", what we would now call post-traumatic stress.
Civilian victims
In 1915 the Ottoman government deported and massacred its Armenian population; most historians call this a genocide, with estimates of the dead ranging from about 600,000 to over a million.
The 1918 flu

The flu spread through troop camps, ships and trains. Unusually, it killed many healthy young adults. In Portugal, where it was called the "pneumónica", it hit in autumn 1918; estimates of deaths start at about 60,000.
The war and the pandemic together made 1914–1920 one of the deadliest periods in modern history.

deep.w: It started in Spain, hence "Spanish flu"
deep.r: Spain was neutral and reported it freely; warring countries censored news, so the name stuck to Spain

cards.title: The Treaty of Versailles
cards.text: The 1919 peace treaty blamed Germany, imposed heavy reparations and took territory. Empires collapsed: Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and the Russian Empire. New nations appeared.

deep.x: The peace conference met in Paris in 1919, dominated by France, Britain and the USA. Germany was not allowed to negotiate. The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919, five years to the day after Sarajevo, in the same Hall of Mirrors where the German Empire had been proclaimed.
Different goals
A new map

Four empires fell: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. New or restored states appeared: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Austria and Hungary became small separate countries. In the Middle East, Britain and France took Ottoman lands as "mandates", drawing borders for Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Palestine.
The League of Nations
US president Woodrow Wilson championed a League of Nations to settle disputes peacefully. But the US Senate refused to ratify the treaty, so the USA never joined, weakening the League from the start.
Portugal attended the conference as one of the victors. It received a small share of reparations and the small Kionga triangle in northern Mozambique.
Versailles redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East, but left Germany humiliated rather than reconciled.

cards.title: Seeds of the next war
cards.text: Resentment in Germany, economic crisis and unresolved disputes helped extremists rise, leading to another world war only 20 years later.

deep.x: Many Germans did not feel defeated: in November 1918 their armies were still on foreign soil. Nationalists spread a myth that the army had been "stabbed in the back" by socialists, Jews and politicians at home. The new democratic Weimar Republic was blamed for signing the treaty.
Money that became paper

In 1923, after Germany fell behind on reparations, France occupied the Ruhr industrial region. The German government printed money to pay striking workers, and prices exploded. Savings were wiped out, hurting the middle classes most.

x: Jan 1923: 1 US dollar ≈ 18,000 marks
Nov 1923: 1 US dollar ≈ 4.2 trillion marks
Prices roughly doubling every few days at the peak

deep.x: Unfinished business
Why it all fell apart

The League of Nations had no army and lacked the USA. When the Great Depression struck in 1929, unemployment helped extremists, above all the Nazis, gain votes. Hitler promised to tear up Versailles, and many Germans believed him.
The First World War did not end the rivalries that caused it; it created new grievances that extremists exploited.
French marshal Ferdinand Foch is said to have called the treaty not a peace but an armistice for twenty years. The Second World War began twenty years and two months later.

quiz.q: What event triggered WWI?
options: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand

quiz.q: Where did Portuguese troops suffer heavy losses on 9 April 1918?
When did the armistice end the fighting?

lessons.title: Between the wars
lessons.summary: Republics, the Depression and dictatorships.

cards.title: The roaring twenties
cards.text: After the war, the 1920s brought jazz, cinema, radio, cars and booming stock markets in the USA, along with new freedoms for women, including the vote in many countries.

deep.x: After the horror of the war and the 1918 flu, many people, especially in American and European cities, wanted to enjoy life. The USA had come out of the war as the world's largest economy and its biggest lender. Mass production made new goods affordable for ordinary families for the first time.
The consumer society

Henry Ford's assembly line cut the time to build a car from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half. About 15 million Model Ts were made by 1927. Buying on credit, "pay as you go", spread to cars, radios and furniture, and advertising grew into an industry.
New freedoms for women
Young women called "flappers" cut their hair short, wore shorter skirts, smoked and danced in public, shocking their parents. More women worked in offices and shops.
The other side

Not everyone roared. American farmers suffered from falling prices, racial segregation was harsh, and the ban on alcohol (Prohibition, 1920–33) fed organised crime. In Germany the decade began with hyperinflation, and in Portugal it was a time of political chaos.
The 1920s created the modern consumer lifestyle, built on new technology, mass culture and credit.
In Portugal, Carolina Beatriz Ângelo voted in 1911, the first woman to vote in southern Europe, using a loophole for literate heads of household; the law was then changed to exclude women.

cards.title: The 1929 crash
cards.text: In October 1929 the New York stock market collapsed. Banks failed, trade shrank and unemployment soared worldwide: the Great Depression.

deep.x: Through the 1920s, share prices on Wall Street soared. Many investors bought shares "on margin", paying perhaps only 10% themselves and borrowing the rest, betting prices would keep rising. When prices began to fall, lenders demanded their money, forcing sales that pushed prices down further.
Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
On 24 October 1929 panic hit the market; on 29 October, "Black Tuesday", it collapsed. But the crash was only the beginning. The Dow Jones index kept sliding for almost three years.

x: Sept 1929 peak: Dow ≈ 381
July 1932 low: Dow ≈ 41
Fall ≈ 89%

deep.x: From crash to Depression

x: About 9,000 American banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out savers
US unemployment rose to about 25% in 1933
Countries raised tariffs to protect their industries, starting with the USA in 1930, so world trade shrank by about two-thirds in value
US banks called back loans from Europe, spreading the crisis, especially to Germany

deep.x: Portugal and the crisis

Portugal's mostly rural and fairly closed economy was hit less than industrial countries, though emigration to Brazil and the USA collapsed and exports suffered. The crisis helped Salazar argue that strict budgets and strong rule were needed.
The crash turned into a Great Depression because banks, trade and spending collapsed together, each making the others worse.

deep.w: The Depression was caused only by the stock crash
deep.r: Bank failures, tight money, the gold standard and trade wars did most of the damage

cards.title: The Soviet Union
cards.text: After the 1917 revolution, the Bolsheviks created the Soviet Union. Under Stalin, forced collectivisation and purges killed millions, including in the Ukrainian famine (Holodomor) of 1932–33.

deep.x: The Bolsheviks seized power in November 1917 and won a brutal civil war (1918–21). In 1922 they created the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). After Lenin's death in 1924, Joseph Stalin outmanoeuvred his rivals and by about 1928 held supreme power.
Industry at any cost

Stalin's Five-Year Plans built steel works, dams and whole new industrial cities at enormous speed. Output of coal, steel and electricity rose sharply, which later helped the USSR survive Hitler's invasion. But the plans relied on forced labour and fear.
Collectivisation and famine

Peasants were forced to give up their land and animals to join collective farms. Those labelled "kulaks", supposedly rich peasants, were deported or shot. Grain was seized for the cities and for export even as harvests failed.

In Ukraine, the Holodomor ("death by hunger") killed roughly 3.5–5 million people; Kazakhstan lost perhaps a third or more of its Kazakh population. Ukraine and many other countries recognise the Holodomor as a genocide.
The Great Terror
Party members, army officers, engineers and ordinary people were arrested on invented charges, forced to confess and shot or sent to Gulag labour camps.
Stalin turned the USSR into an industrial power through terror, famine and forced labour that killed millions of its own people.
Soviet censors routinely erased purged officials from photographs, so that people "disappeared" from history as well as from life.

cards.title: Fascism in Italy
cards.text: Mussolini took power in 1922 and built a one-party state with censorship, a personality cult and aggressive nationalism: fascism.

deep.x: Italy was on the winning side in 1918, but many Italians felt cheated: the peace gave them less territory than promised, and the economy was in trouble. Strikes and factory occupations in 1919–20 frightened landowners and industrialists, who feared a communist revolution.
The march on Rome

Benito Mussolini, a former socialist journalist, founded the fascist movement in 1919. His "blackshirt" squads beat and killed socialists and burned union offices. In October 1922, as fascists gathered to march on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III refused to use the army against them and asked Mussolini to form a government.
What fascism meant

In 1924 the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti, who denounced fascist violence, was murdered. Within two years opposition parties were banned. In 1929 Mussolini made peace with the Pope, creating the Vatican City state. In 1935–36 Italy invaded Ethiopia, using poison gas.
A model for others

x: The name comes from the "fasces", a bundle of rods carried in ancient Rome as a symbol of authority
Fascist movements copied Mussolini across Europe, from Germany to Spain
Salazar admired some of his methods but kept his own distance from fascist mass politics

deep.x: Fascism was born in Italy: a violent, nationalist movement that took power legally and then destroyed democracy from within.

deep.w: Mussolini made the trains run on time
deep.r: It was mostly propaganda; much railway improvement predated him

cards.title: Hitler's rise
cards.text: In Germany, the Depression helped the Nazi party grow. Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and quickly destroyed democracy, persecuted Jews and opponents, and rearmed.

deep.x: Adolf Hitler, an Austrian-born former corporal, led a small party of extremists that tried and failed to seize power in Munich in 1923. In prison he wrote Mein Kampf, setting out his racism and plans for conquest. For most of the 1920s the Nazis were a fringe party.
How the Depression helped

With six million unemployed, many voters turned to parties promising radical change: the Nazis and the communists. The Nazis blamed Versailles, communists and Jews, and promised jobs, order and national pride. They never won a majority in a free election.
From chancellor to dictator
Conservative politicians persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933, believing they could control him. They were wrong.

After a fire at the parliament building, civil liberties were suspended. The Enabling Act let Hitler make laws without parliament. Unions and other parties were abolished, and the first concentration camp opened at Dachau in March 1933.
Persecution and rearmament

x: Jews were boycotted, expelled from jobs and, from 1935, stripped of citizenship
On Kristallnacht in November 1938, synagogues burned across Germany
Conscription returned in 1935 and military spending soared, which reduced unemployment

deep.x: Hitler came to power through elections and a backroom deal, then used legal powers to destroy democracy in months.

deep.w: Hitler was elected by a majority of Germans
deep.r: The Nazis' best free result was 37%; he was appointed by elites who thought they could use him

cards.title: The First Portuguese Republic
cards.text: The monarchy fell on 5 October 1910. The First Republic separated church and state and expanded education, but was unstable: 45 governments in 16 years.

deep.x: By 1910 the monarchy had lost much of its support, weakened by the 1890 Ultimatum, debt and the assassination of King Carlos and his heir in 1908. On 4 October 1910 republicans and rebel sailors rose in Lisbon. The next morning, 5 October, the Republic was proclaimed from the balcony of Lisbon's city hall, and King Manuel II sailed into exile in England.
Big ambitions
Republicans wanted a modern, secular, educated nation. About 70–75% of adults could not read, so schools were a priority. The new flag in green and red and the anthem "A Portuguesa" date from 1911.
Why it struggled

x: Clashes with the Catholic Church alienated much of the rural population
Voting was limited, mostly to literate men, so few took part
The First World War brought debt, hunger and the CEP disaster
Coups, bombs and strikes were frequent; in 1918 President Sidónio Pais was assassinated, and in 1921 the prime minister was murdered

deep.x: The First Republic modernised laws and symbols that last to this day, but never achieved stable government.
Today's 5 October public holiday, the flag and the national anthem all come from the First Republic.

cards.title: The Estado Novo begins
cards.text: After a military coup in 1926, finance minister António de Oliveira Salazar became prime minister in 1932 and created the Estado Novo, an authoritarian, corporatist regime with censorship and a political police (PVDE, later PIDE).

deep.x: On 28 May 1926 General Gomes da Costa marched from Braga, and the military took power with little resistance; many Portuguese were tired of chaos. But the generals could not fix the finances. In 1928 they appointed António de Oliveira Salazar, an economics professor from Coimbra, as finance minister, with a veto over every ministry's spending.
The "New State"

Salazar balanced the budget within a year, which won him prestige. As prime minister from 1932, he introduced a constitution in 1933, approved in a plebiscite in which abstentions were counted as votes in favour.
How it controlled society

x: The censors' "blue pencil" cut newspapers, books, plays and films
The political police (PVDE, renamed PIDE in 1945) used informers, torture and prison
In 1936 a prison camp opened at Tarrafal in Cape Verde, where dozens of prisoners died
Corporatism replaced free unions with state-run bodies; strikes were illegal
Youth were enrolled in the Mocidade Portuguesa

deep.x: Fascist or not?
Historians debate the label. Salazar preferred a quiet, Catholic, rural order and distrusted mass mobilisation, but his regime was clearly authoritarian.
The Estado Novo traded freedom for order, and lasted 48 years, from the 1926 coup to 1974.
Salazar rarely travelled abroad and never flew in an aeroplane, a symbol of his inward-looking rule.

cards.title: The Spanish Civil War
cards.text: From 1936 to 1939, Spain's republic fought Franco's nationalists, who were helped by Germany and Italy. Franco won and ruled Spain until 1975. Portugal's regime supported Franco.

deep.x: Spain became a republic in 1931. Its reforms on land, the Church and the army divided the country. In February 1936 a left-wing Popular Front won elections. In July, army generals, including Francisco Franco, launched a coup. It succeeded in some regions and failed in others, and Spain split in two.
A rehearsal for world war

Germany sent the Condor Legion of aircraft and pilots, and Italy sent tens of thousands of soldiers. The Soviet Union sold weapons to the Republic, and about 35,000–40,000 foreign volunteers fought in the International Brigades. Britain and France stayed out under a non-intervention policy that in practice hurt the Republic.
Portugal's role

Salazar feared a left-wing Spain would spread revolution to Portugal. He let supplies reach Franco through Portugal, sent volunteers known as "Viriatos" and backed the nationalists diplomatically. After the massacre in Badajoz in 1936, some refugees who fled across the border were handed back to Franco's forces. In 1939 the two dictatorships signed the Iberian Pact of friendship.
The cost
Estimates of the dead range up to about 500,000, including mass executions on both sides. Some 450,000 refugees fled to France in early 1939, and Franco's repression continued for years.
The Spanish Civil War was a brutal national conflict and a testing ground for the weapons and alliances of the Second World War.
Picasso painted Guernica in 1937 in response to the bombing of the Basque town; the painting returned to Spain only in 1981, after democracy was restored.

cards.title: The New Deal
cards.text: In the USA, Roosevelt's New Deal created public works, social security and bank regulation to fight the Depression, expanding the role of government.

deep.x: Franklin D. Roosevelt became US president in March 1933, at the depth of the Depression. A quarter of workers were jobless, and banks were closing across the country. He promised "a new deal for the American people" and launched a burst of laws in his first hundred days.
What it created

x: The Civilian Conservation Corps employed about 3 million young men planting forests and building parks
The Tennessee Valley Authority built dams that brought electricity to poor rural areas
The SEC was created to police the stock market

deep.x: Did it work?

Unemployment fell from about 25% in 1933 to about 14% in 1937, then rose again when spending was cut too soon. Full recovery came only with massive spending for the Second World War. Economists still argue about which policies helped most.
A lasting change

The New Deal established that national governments are responsible for protecting people from economic disaster. In 1936 the economist John Maynard Keynes argued that governments should spend more in slumps, an idea that shaped policy for decades.
The New Deal saved American democracy in a time of crisis by making government a safety net, not just a referee.
Roosevelt's radio "fireside chats" explained his policies directly to millions of listeners in their homes.

cards.title: Appeasement
cards.text: Britain and France tried to avoid war by giving in to Hitler's demands, accepting Austria's annexation and, at Munich in 1938, part of Czechoslovakia. It failed.

deep.x: Appeasement meant avoiding war by meeting what seemed like reasonable demands. Many in Britain felt Versailles had been too harsh, and almost everyone dreaded a repeat of the trenches. Britain and France were also slow to rearm and worried about their empires.
Munich, 1938

Hitler demanded the Sudetenland, a border region of Czechoslovakia with many German speakers. On 29–30 September 1938, Britain's Neville Chamberlain and France's Édouard Daladier met Hitler and Mussolini in Munich and agreed to hand it over. Czechoslovakia was not invited. Chamberlain returned promising "peace for our time".
Why it failed

In March 1939 Hitler seized the rest of Czechoslovakia, showing that his aims went far beyond German-speaking lands. Britain and France now guaranteed Poland. In August Hitler and Stalin signed a non-aggression pact, secretly dividing eastern Europe between them.
The lesson drawn

items.r: Some leaders read them as weakness

deep.x: Ever since, "Munich" and "appeasement" have been used as warnings, sometimes too quickly, whenever leaders debate standing up to an aggressor.
Appeasement failed because Hitler wanted not fair borders but conquest, and each concession made him bolder.

deep.w: Chamberlain was a fool who believed Hitler completely
deep.r: He was also rearming, especially the air force, which helped Britain survive in 1940

quiz.q: When was the Portuguese republic proclaimed?
What began in October 1929?
options: The Great Depression, with the Wall Street crash
